stops.name: Magdalen College, the friendship with C. S. Lewis
stops.campa: At a meeting of the English faculty Tolkien first meets a stocky, argumentative young don from Magdalen, Clive Staples Lewis. They fall into deep talk, and one September night walking on Addison's Walk they argue until the small hours about myth: Tolkien holding that myths are not lies but broken lights of the true, and that in Christ the great myth had become fact. Lewis, an atheist, is moved toward belief. The two become the closest of friends and each other's chief encouragers; without Lewis's cheering-on, Tolkien later says, The Lord of the Rings would never have been finished.
stops.quote: The unpayable debt that I owe to him was not 'influence' as it is ordinarily understood, but sheer encouragement. He was for long my only audience.

stops.name: 20 Northmoor Road, the blank page and the hobbit
stops.campa: One summer in his study at Northmoor Road, marking a great weary heap of School Certificate papers, Tolkien turns a page and finds one candidate has left a leaf blank. Onto that emptiness, without thought or plan, he writes: 'In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.' He does not know what a hobbit is, and so must find out. From that single unwilled sentence grows a story he tells his children by the fire: of Bilbo Baggins, the dragon Smaug, the ring found in the dark. And, unlooked-for, the door into all of Middle-earth swings open for the world to enter.
stops.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit. Not a nasty, dirty, wet hole, filled with the ends of worms and an oozy smell . . . it was a hobbit-hole, and that means comfort.

stops.name: The Hobbit published, the world enters Middle-earth
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of September, George Allen & Unwin of London publish The Hobbit, or There and Back Again, with the author's own maps and pictures. Stanley Unwin's small son Rayner, given the manuscript to judge for a shilling, has approved it. The book is an immediate success; the publisher, hungry for more, asks for a sequel about hobbits. Tolkien, hoping instead to give them his great mythology of the Silmarils, is turned back toward the little folk, and so, that winter, sits down to write what he thinks a short sequel, not knowing it will take him seventeen years and become The Lord of the Rings.
stops.quote: One writes such a story not out of the leaves of trees still to be observed . . . but it grows like a seed in the dark out of the leaf-mould of the mind.

stops.name: University of St Andrews, the Andrew Lang lecture on Faërie
stops.campa: Before the University of St Andrews, Tolkien delivers the Andrew Lang lecture, 'On Fairy-Stories', and sets out the whole theology of his art. The teller of tales, he says, is a sub-creator, making a Secondary World the mind may enter and believe, an act that images the making of the great Creator whose child he is. And there is a good catastrophe, a eucatastrophe: the sudden joyous turn beyond hope that marks the true fairy-story. The Gospels hold the greatest of these: the Birth of Christ is the eucatastrophe of Man's history, the Resurrection its crown. His whole legendarium is here confessed as a work of faith.
stops.quote: The Birth of Christ is the eucatastrophe of Man's history. The Resurrection is the eucatastrophe of the story of the Incarnation. This story begins and ends in joy.

stops.name: The Eagle and Child, the Inklings in the Rabbit Room
stops.campa: On Tuesday mornings a company of friends gathers in the small back parlour of the Eagle and Child in St Giles': the pub they fondly call the Bird and Baby, the room the Rabbit Room. Here Lewis, Charles Williams, Hugo Dyson, Owen Barfield, Warnie Lewis and Tolkien drink beer, argue, and read aloud their works in progress. In this snug the world first hears, chapter by halting chapter, the tale of the Ring; here Narnia too is first spoken. The Inklings are the second and greatest Fellowship of his life: a company of makers, the T.C.B.S. reborn and, this time, surviving.

stops.name: Merton College, the New Hobbit across seventeen years
stops.campa: Through the years of the Second War and after, in his study and among the Inklings, Tolkien labours at the sequel that keeps deepening and darkening until it is no children's tale but a vast heroic romance of a Ring of Power that must be unmade. In 1945 he is elected Merton Professor of English Language and Literature. The writing is slow, halting, abandoned and resumed across seventeen years; he despairs of it, revises endlessly, redraws his maps, works out the calendars and tongues behind every page. It is, he knows, the labour of his life: the great tale grown at last out of all the smaller ones.
stops.quote: I do not think that even Power or Domination is the real centre of my story. . . . The real theme for me is about something much more permanent and difficult: Death and Immortality.

stops.name: The Fellowship of the Ring published, the great tale comes forth
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of July, Allen & Unwin bring out The Fellowship of the Ring, first volume of The Lord of the Rings, with The Two Towers to follow in November and The Return of the King the next year. The publisher fears it will lose money; instead it slowly, then swiftly, conquers. Into it Tolkien has poured everything: the Shire that is Sarehole, the fallen friends who are Frodo's companions, the batmen who are Sam, the Marshes that are the Somme, the invented tongues and the runes, the long defeat lit by sudden grace. The mythology dreamed with the immortal four is given at last to the world.
stops.quote: I am in fact a Hobbit (in all but size). I like gardens, trees, and unmechanized farmlands . . . I like, and even dare to wear in these dull days, ornamental waistcoats.

stops.name: The Return of the King, the eucatastrophe and the Grey Havens
stops.campa: On the twentieth of October the third volume, The Return of the King, completes the tale, and with it the appendices: the calendars, the family trees, and the tables of the Tengwar and the Cirth laboured over for years. The Ring is unmade at the crack of doom by the failure of the very hobbit who bore it, and grace turns ruin to victory: the eucatastrophe he preached at St Andrews, made flesh. At the last, Frodo the wounded goes down to the Grey Havens and sails west over sea, into the light beyond the world's edge, healed of a hurt that will not heal on earth.
stops.quote: The grey rain-curtain turned all to silver glass and was rolled back, and he beheld white shores and beyond them a far green country under a swift sunrise.
stops.quote_source: The Return of the King, 'The Grey Havens'

stops.name: Poole and the Hotel Miramar, the retreat from fame
stops.campa: Grown famous beyond bearing, besieged by admirers who telephone in the night and camp on his lawn, Tolkien takes Edith away to the mild seaside air of Poole, near Bournemouth, for her failing health. They live quietly in a bungalow; he keeps his study and his pipe and his invented alphabets; they holiday at the Hotel Miramar overlooking the sea. It is a kind of exile from Oxford, borne for love of her. The great work is done; the tales of the Elder Days he still cannot finish lie in their boxes. He waits, like his own Elves, at the shore of the world, near the end of an age.

stops.name: Wolvercote Cemetery, Edith as Lúthien upon the stone
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of November Edith dies at eighty-two. Tolkien, broken, returns to Oxford, to rooms Merton gives him. Upon her grave in the Catholic ground of Wolvercote he has cut, beneath her name, the single word Lúthien, for she was, and knew she was, his Lúthien, who danced for him among the hemlocks fifty years before. He writes to his son that he cannot now plead before the inexorable Mandos, lord of the dead, for the return of the one he loved; the story has gone crooked, and he is left behind, as Beren was left when Lúthien first died.
stops.quote: I never called Edith Lúthien — but she was the source of the story that in time became the chief part of the Silmarillion. . . . For she was (and knew she was) my Lúthien.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 340 (to Christopher Tolkien, 11 July 1972)

stops.name: Bournemouth, the passing of the maker
stops.campa: Visiting friends in Bournemouth, Tolkien is taken with a bleeding ulcer and then a chest infection, and on the second of September, one-and-twenty months after Edith, he dies at eighty-one. He is buried with her in the single grave at Wolvercote, and beneath his name is added the word Beren, so that the mortal man and the immortal maid lie together under the names of his own most beloved tale, made true at the last. He believed that beyond the circles of the world there was more than memory; that the fallen maker of secondary worlds might himself be a strand in the great Story still being told.
stops.quote: But all the stars are one to me; nor light of Sun nor moon I know, till on the hither shore once more I find the Haven long ago . . .
stops.quote_source: Tolkien, 'The Sea-Bell' (The Adventures of Tom Bombadil)

stops.name: The Silmarillion, the great mythology given to the world
stops.campa: Four years after his father's death, Christopher Tolkien brings out at last The Silmarillion: the vast mythology of the Elder Days that Tolkien laboured over from the wards of the Great War until his death and never could finish. Here are the Music of the Ainur by which the world is sung into being, the theft of the Silmarils, the wars against Morgoth, and Beren and Lúthien at the centre, begun in a hemlock glade in 1917. The work dreamed with the immortal four, held as a debt to the dead across sixty years, comes forth complete. The maker has passed over sea, but the sub-creation stands.
stops.quote: There was Eru, the One, who in Arda is called Ilúvatar; and he made first the Ainur, the Holy Ones, that were the offspring of his thought.
